name: The Bar That Dates The Window Wrong
aka: Georgian bar on a Federal house
symptom: The light count and the sash proportion are right for the style, but the bar is visibly heavy. On a Federal or Greek Revival elevation the bar measures 1 1/8 to 1 1/4 in where it should be 5/8 to 7/8 in; the grid reads as a dark lattice rather than as thin lines, and at fifty feet the window looks fifty years older than the house.

cause.explanation: The insulated glass unit sets the floor. A sealed unit needs an edge seal of about 5/8 in that must be concealed, so the narrowest bar that can conceal an edge seal on both sides of a joint in a true divided assembly is about 1 1/8 in, and manufacturers state this directly — Kolbe's true divided lite is a 1 1/8 in wood bar and not narrower. The bar is not chosen; it is what the sealed unit leaves. Sash depth follows: 1 3/8 in historic becomes 1 3/4 in or more.
cause.cost_saved: Nothing at the bar. The driver is thermal code compliance, which requires the sealed unit, which requires the bar. This is a fault produced by a requirement rather than by an economy, which is why it is the hardest one in the openings group to argue away.

rule_violated.statement: muntin width 7/8 in; sash depth 1 3/8 in. The pack's own note: the muntin section dates a window more reliably than the light count, because light counts were revived and muntin sections mostly were not.
Muntins no wider than 7/8 in. Muntins at Georgian width, 1 1/4 in and up, collapse the style at any distance beyond fifty feet.
A true divided insulated unit forces 1 1/8 to 1 1/4 in.

correct_practice: Know which number the style is asking for before choosing the glazing. Georgian and earlier: 7/8 to 1 in, with 12/12 or 9/9 sash and small lights. Federal and Regency: 5/8 to 7/8 in, fewer and larger lights, 6/6 or 6/9. Greek Revival: back toward 7/8 to 1 in with 6/6 and larger glass again. Craftsman and Prairie: 1 1/8 in and up, deliberately. If the style wants a bar under 7/8 in, an insulated true divided light cannot supply it, and the honest routes are a single-glazed sash with an interior storm panel — which reaches an assembly U of about 0.35 — or a simulated assembly whose exterior bar is made to the correct width regardless of the seal behind it.

fixes.right: Single-glazed true divided sash at the historic bar width, with a well-fitted interior storm panel or an interior secondary sash. This preserves the diagnostic dimension and reaches thermal parity with a standard double-glazed unit.
fixes.cheap: Keep the sealed unit and reduce the light count so the wide bar has a job to do. A 6/6 sash at 1 1/8 in bars is a defensible mid-nineteenth-century window; a 12/12 at 1 1/8 in is a lattice. Changing the count costs nothing and moves the window to a date the bar can actually support.
fixes.dishonest: Specifying a narrow simulated bar over a sealed unit whose spacer is wider than the bar. The spacer then shows as a grey line either side of the muntin and the window reads as having a triple bar, which is a period impossibility and looks it.

detection: Measure the bar against the glass in a photograph: express bar width as a fraction of light width. A Georgian 9 in light with a 7/8 in bar gives about 0.10; the same light with a 1 1/4 in bar gives 0.14, and the grid darkens visibly. Cross-check against the style's date: if the elevation carries a fanlight, thin cornice and graduated storey heights — Federal signals — and the bar is heavy, the fault is present. Also compare against the sash stile: the historic stile is about 2 in and the bar 7/8 in, a ratio of 2.3; when the bar has been fattened by the sealed unit the ratio falls toward 1.6 and the grid competes with the frame.

exceptions.why: The style's own constraint sets a floor, not a ceiling: muntins not less than 1 1/8 in wide, vertical, three or four per upper sash. A thin bar is the fault here, not a wide one.
exceptions.bounds: Vertical bars in the upper sash only, lower sash a single light. Width 1 1/8 to 1 3/8 in. This does not licence a wide bar in a horizontal grid.

bounds_test.note: Style floor. Vertical bars in the upper sash only, 1 1/8 to 1 3/8 in; the lower sash is a single light.

exceptions.why: Rectilinear art glass with came or wide wood bars is the idiom; the bar is a compositional line and its weight is the point.
exceptions.bounds: Casement sash, rectilinear geometry, no curves, bands with continuous head and sill courses.

bounds_test.note: Casement sash, rectilinear geometry, no curves, bands with continuous head and sill courses. Any curve in the pattern voids the exception.

exceptions.why: Leaded glazing uses lead came of 1/4 to 3/8 in face width in diamond or rectangular quarries, which is a different family of dimension entirely and is not measured against sash-bar rules.
exceptions.bounds: True lead came in a glazed panel set into a casement, not a bar imitating came. Where a Tudor Revival house uses double-hung sash, the sash-bar rules apply again.

bounds_test.note: True lead came in a leaded panel set into a casement. Outside 1/4 to 3/8 in it is not came, and a came-pattern grille between panes is a different fault entirely.

applies_when.note: Depends on the glazing being real leaded panel in a casement. Where a Tudor Revival house uses double-hung sash, the sash-bar rules apply again in full.

exceptions.why: The revival itself ran 7/8 in and wider against the eighteenth century's nearer 5/8 in, and that heaviness is a documented characteristic of the revival rather than a modern error.
exceptions.bounds: Legitimate on a house dated and detailed as Colonial Revival — that is, one that also carries the revival's larger entry surround and its 6/6 or 6/1 sash. It is not a licence on a house claiming an eighteenth-century date.

bounds_test.note: The revival's own band runs 7/8 in and up with 6/6, 8/8 or 6/1 sash. The licence is void on a house claiming an eighteenth-century date, which is the bound that matters.

applies_when.note: The licence is for work honestly presented as of the revival period, carrying the revival's larger entry surround and its own sash patterns.

confused_with.difference: Width versus depth. A correct 7/8 in bar with no setback still fails at distance; a 1 1/4 in bar with a full moulded setback reads well but reads as the wrong period.
Count versus section. The pack's own claim is that the section is the more reliable date evidence, because counts were revived and sections were not.

sources: Kolbe true divided lite specification, 1 1/8 in wood muntin bar

test.note: The scale-free form, which works from a photograph without knowing the opening size. A 9 in Georgian light with a 7/8 in bar gives 0.097; the same light with a 1 1/4 in bar gives 0.139 and the grid visibly darkens. This is the ratio the eye is actually reading.

secondary_tests.note: The absolute band for Anglo-American work before about 1850. Federal and Regency sit at the bottom of it, Georgian and Greek Revival at the top. Craftsman, Prairie and any post-1900 idiom are outside it by intention and should be evaluated against their own floors instead.

Historic: 7/8 against a 2 in stile, about 0.44. When the sealed unit fattens the bar the stile is widened with it, so this ratio holds and the grid coarsens together — which is why it is a poor primary test and a useful confirmation that the whole sash has been scaled up rather than just the bar.

severity_by_style.why: The style's constraint states that muntins at Georgian width, 1 1/4 in and up, collapse the style at any distance beyond fifty feet.
Bars heavier than 18 mm date the work to before 1780 and remove the sheet-of-light reading the style depends on.
The revival itself ran 7/8 in and wider against the eighteenth century's nearer 5/8 in, and that heaviness is a documented characteristic of the revival rather than a modern error.
The style's floor is 1 1/8 in; a wide bar is the requirement, not the fault.
Wide bars and came in rectilinear art glass are the idiom.

inverted_by.statement: Here the fault is a bar narrower than 1 1/8 in. The style's constraint sets a floor and no ceiling, and a thin equal grid is the Craftsman failure.
A slight bar is the fault; the bar's weight is the composition.
The dimension inverts entirely: lead came at 1/4 to 3/8 in face width is a different family, and a sash bar imitating came at 7/8 in is the fault.
